In my first year of college, I was required to take Cultural Communications. It was a very basic course that taught you social taboos and norms among other basic things. My instructor separated the class into about 6-7 different groups, and handed us each a packet containing a deck of cards and the rules to a particular card game we had to play in complete silence. After reading the rules, the paper had to be placed back into the envelope.

The winner had to move clockwise to the next table, while the loser had to move counter clockwise to the closest table (The tables made a circular formation in the room). Again, this all had to be completed without any of the students verbalizing.

At first, the instructor made it sound like we were all playing the exact same game, but it was actually the complete opposite. No two card games were the same. After the first loser and winner rotation occurred, (Me losing! Yay!) I remember starting up the second round of card games by placing my card down. and everyone in the new group stared at it silently for the longest time before slowly lifting their gazes in unison towards me with much confusion on their faces.

I caught on at that moment, and proceeded to throw in a random card each time. You could hear lots of giggling, as well as frustrated gestures through the room. After about 3 or 4 rotations, each card game became a giant catastrophic mess of misunderstanding. Those who never rotated were hell-bent on trying to find a way to let other players know that they were incorrectly grabbing cards from the hands played, and they were actually the winner. I saw some people yank cards away from others, and it was starting to get fairly ugly.

Once our instructor told us to stop, and return to our normally assigned seats to discuss this, the frustration turned into laughter and everyone feeling more at ease.

The lesson or concept my instructor tried to show us was based on norms and taboos, and how many of our socially accepted rules are quite different and can easily be misinterpreted. I also was able to see just how frustrating language barriers could be.

I felt the instructor made her point very clear in a way we could all actually experience it.
What was a creative, engaging and memorable way an instructor/teacher managed to teach you a lesson or concept?

This technique was something another student brought up in my teaching math class about repeating decimals. So if you wanted to write something like .37121212... in fraction form how would you do it? Well, everyone had different approaches as you might expect. But one student had this really impressive algorithm to figure this out. She said :

  1. take the non-repeating part of the decimal
    37
  2. count how many digits the repeating portion is
    2
  3. count how many digits the non-repeating portion is
    2
  4. multiply the nonrepeating portion by a string of 9's repeating as many times as the number from step 2
    (37 x 99)
  5. add this to the repeating digits
    (37 x 99 + 12)
  6. divide by the a string with as many 9's as the number from step 2 followed by as many 0's as the number from step 3 so,
    (37 x 99 + 12)/9900

and the result is .37121212...

You can really see how they derived this by
37/100 + (12/99)(1/100) =
37(99)/9900 + 12/9900 =
(39 x 99 + 12)/9900.

This was mindblowing because no one in a class of 40 knew about this algorithm until she showed us. Branching off this, we had a lot of examples about how to prove that dividing 9 would yield a repeating decimal and someone proved it using the infinite geometric series formula a/(1-r) because the ratio would be .1 and a would be the number that's repeating. So .111... would be
.1/(1-.1) = 1/9.
